title: Good Hendrik
sentences: The favourable reception which my little Readers' Books have generally enjoyed among Teachers
encouraged me to fill the gap between the Primer or First Reader and the Reader for the second class
with several others, and thus, as far as order is concerned, to supply as complete a set of Readers as possible.
The little work which, under the title above, I offer to my fellow-teachers follows in rank upon the said Primer or First Reader.
Much might I say about the choice of subject and of form,
if a work of this kind could admit such a digression.
I need only remark that I have refrained from everything exaggerated; that I have spoken of no virtues
beyond a child's reach, nor mentioned vices that may still be unknown to them;
while I have tried to provide as much variety as the subject in any way allows.
That this attempt may further prove useful to youth is the wish of the
author.
Do you not know Hendrik, who always takes off his hat so politely when he passes by?
Many people call him good Hendrik, because he is so obedient and because he behaves so kindly toward everyone.
He never harms anyone.
There are children who do not love him.
Yes, but those are naughty children.
All good children are glad to be with Hendrik.
Children who keep company with Hendrik become even better, for they learn from him how they ought to behave.
If Hendrik is so good, he will surely love his parents too.
All good children love their parents.
Yes, he loves his parents very much; that is why he is always so cheerful and content.
He gets no dainty food and drink, and he has no fine clothes: how then can he be so content?
Do you believe that one must have dainty food and drink and fine clothes to be content?
— I do not.
But there comes Hendrik; we shall ask him ourselves.
Ha!
good morning, friend Hendrik!
How is it that you are always so cheerful and content?
Well, that is a strange question.
Are you not satisfied?
I have everything I need; should I not then be cheerful and content?
Yes, but you have no dainty food and drink.
Eh!
are you such a friend of dainty food and drink?
I enjoy it too.
But my father says that the daintiest food and drink is often harmful,
and that one must be moderate to stay healthy.
I believe your father is only making things up for you.
No, my father does not do that.
He says it for my good.
He also knows better what is useful to me than I do.
Hendrik has no fine clothes,
but they are always equally neat.
— One never sees a spot on them.
What is the reason that Hendrik always appears so tidy?
His parents surely buy him new clothes often.
No, they do not.
— I asked his little brother about it lately, and he told me
that his brother always takes care not to neglect his clothes.
When he undresses in the evening, he lays his things neatly on a chair.
He never lets his clothes wander about the room, as slovenly children do.
I was at Hendrik's home lately, and you should have seen how obedient he is to his parents.
When they tell him to do something, he does it at once.
He never waits until they tell him twice.
let my brother or sister do it; but he is always glad when he can do something for his dear parents.
When they forbid him something, he stops at once.
why must I stop?
He never looks sulky when his parents forbid him something.
I praised Hendrik for his obedience, but he would hear nothing of it.
What do you think he answered me?
My parents know very well why they command or forbid me something.
They know well what is useful or harmful to me.
Fie!
should I be disobedient?
Should I grieve my parents?
When I was disobedient once lately, tears stood in my mother's
eyes; but I shall take care that it does not happen again.
but I resolved henceforth to be as obedient as Hendrik.
Hendrik must often play with his little brothers and his sister, and he does so gladly.
When Hendrik has run an errand and comes home again, they stretch out their little hands to him,
for they love to play with Hendrik, because he is so kind and accommodating.
You should see him play with his little brothers and his sister; then you would gladly join in too.
He never grumbles.
When they ask him for some toy, and when they may have it,
he gives it to them, and then they play together.
Hendrik thinks: I am the oldest, and ought also to be the wisest.
Will you buy nice apples too, young gentlemen?
No, ma'am!
How much are the apples?
A cent apiece.
Come, give me then for a stiver.
Will you have some for a stiver too?
No, ma'am!
I do not buy apples.
Do you want me to lend you a stiver?
I thank you, my boy!
I have a stiver, but I may not eat sweets.
Is it then eating sweets when one spends one's money on apples?
Your father does not know it, after all?
My father has forbidden it, and then I do not do it, even when he is not there.
My father says that God sees everything.
May you then buy nothing with your money?
Yes indeed, provided it is useful to me; and then my parents buy it for me.
My mother often gives me good, ripe fruit; but to take it without asking
or quietly to spend my money on such things — that I may not do.
I am glad that my father is not so angry with me.
My father is always good and kind toward me, but ....
Your father is quite right, young sir!
for nothing good ever comes of a sweet-tooth.
When Jakob was still small, he could never leave any delicacies untouched; he always had to taste some.
Then he would nibble the sugar, then lick the syrup,
then take an apple, then again a pear from his mother.
He was often punished for his nibbling, but it did no good.
He spent all his money on sweet-
eating, and the more he did so, the more he craved to nibble.
When he took something he might not have, his heart would beat; then he was anxious and afraid
that his parents would discover it, but that did no good — he went on just the same.
When Jakob was older, he went into service with a gentleman.
He could not break this harmful habit, and when he had eaten up all his money, he knew no way out.
He could not leave off nibbling,
and then he did it all the more from the food and drink prepared for his master.
Once he had gone so far that his master discovered it, and he was driven from his service.
The gentleman pitied him, therefore he did not tell other people.
Now Jakob went about earning nothing.
His parents had long been dead, and he had to suffer want in everything.
Fortunately he came to his senses about his bad habit in time.
He saw for himself how harmful nibbling is.
He mended his ways and was afterwards taken into service by another gentleman.
Now he had learned by loss, and took care not to fall into this evil again.
As soon as Hendrik rises in the morning, he thinks with joy of God,
because he receives so much good from Him, and because God keeps him so graciously.
When he reflects on all this, he becomes very glad, because God is so good.
Then he folds his hands together and prays reverently:
I thank Thee that Thou hast preserved me again this night.
Wilt
Thou also this day, and always, keep me graciously, that I may always live aright, and thank Thee for Thy goodness.
Amen.
When he has finished his prayer, he washes and dresses himself,
and gladly does everything his parents ask of him.
I was at Hendrik's parents' for dinner lately; you should have seen how orderly everything went.
Hendrik, who is the oldest, had to say grace aloud.
He stood reverently before the table.
His little brothers and his sister folded their hands, and Hendrik prayed:
Good God!
Thou givest us food.
We thank Thee for it.
Pour Thy blessing thereon, that after partaking of this food we may find ourselves healthy and strengthened.
Amen.
No child touched the food before his parents had given it to him.
When they wanted more, they asked for it very politely.
They did not look discontented when one received more than another.
Each child was doubly content with what his parents gave him.
When they had finished eating, Hendrik gave thanks:
Good God!
Thou hast strengthened us with meat and drink, and thereby given us new strength, that each might perform his work.
Grant us further Thy blessing, and make us thankful for all we receive from Thy goodness.
Amen.
In the evening Hendrik sits with his little brothers and his sister beside his parents.
The father then tells them much that is good, and teaches them how they must behave to become good people.
The children sit then with open mouths listening, for they would gladly become good.
The father then often speaks of God.
He tells his children how good God is, and how much we have to thank Him for.
Before Hendrik goes to bed, he always thanks God for His goodness, and prays that He will keep him through the night too.
Sometimes the father sings an evening hymn with his children.
Then they all think of God, and rejoice because He is so good.
O!
to think of God while singing makes us truly glad.
A child as good as Hendrik will also gladly go to school.
Do not doubt it.
Every good child knows well that much that is useful is to be learned at school.
Hendrik seldom misses a school hour.
He is always glad to be at school, and there is as obedient as at home with his parents.
He never grieves his teacher.
He always knows his lessons.
The teacher never needs to say to him: Hendrik!
pay attention!
When other children talk during the lesson, he asks them not to do so;
but he never tells the teacher when they talk together.
He knows well that this looks very ugly.
He is also not glad when another is punished.
Hendrik went to school lately.
On the way he met Jan, one of his schoolmates.
This one looked so red in the face, and fire shone from his eyes.
What ails you,
Jan!
are you ill?
No!
But that Willem, that bad, naughty boy, he ....
if he were here, I would beat him so that ....
Fie!
how you rage so.
— How can you become so angry?
Would you not become angry too?
— He threw my book in the mud.
But I shall tell the teacher, and then ....
And then?
Then you perhaps think the teacher will punish him.
Why yes!
does he not deserve it?
To throw my book in the mud like that!
It is possible the teacher will punish him,
but he will not do so before he knows whether Willem is to blame.
Did Willem do it out of malice?
I do not know; but see how my book looks!
If Willem is punished by the teacher, will your book thereby become clean?
No, it will not.
or would you gladly see him punished?
Why yes!
for then he would not do it again.
Willem surely did this with no inten-
tion; I know him better.
Could you now rejoice if he were punished innocently?
— Oh no!
do not do this.
No one would praise your conduct.
You would be discontented with yourself, and Willem would surely not love you for it.
But may he then do harm?
No, he may not.
But are you convinced that he did it out of malice?
No.
But what shall I say when the teacher sees my book?
Give me your book — there, take mine.
I shall answer for it; but say nothing about what Willem did
Hendrik quietly laid the book before him on the desk; but it was not
long before the teacher noticed how dirty it looked.
How now, Hendrik!
is your book so dirty?
How does that come?
Teacher!
Willem let it fall on the ground by accident.
But it is not your book; here stands Jan's name: how did you get this book?
I exchanged with Jan, teacher!
Why did you do that?
Teacher!
because Jan was afraid he would get a scolding.
Were you then not afraid of a scolding?
No, teacher!
Because it was an accident, I thought you would say nothing about it.
You behave well, my dear boy!
that you wish to free another — for that you did it — and still better, because you speak the truth.
Such children I love dearly.
It is always good when one speaks the truth.
Come, I shall tell you an example of that once.
Maria, a girl of ten years, was playing once with the maid,
and by mischance let her doll fall on some porcelain on the table, whereby several cups were broken.
Maria was very dismayed, and the maid no less.
She never gladly caused her mother any damage or grief.
At this noise her mother came into the room, and began sharply to scold the maid,
because she thought the maid had broken the things.
She told her she must pay for everything.
The maid was very embarrassed, and kept silent, because she did not wish to tell on Maria.
Maria might now have kept silent too, for her mother had no suspicion of her; but she could not.
Her heart told her she would then act very badly.
She fell around her mother's neck and cried, sobbing: oh, dear mother!
forgive me!
the maid did not do it, but I broke it.
It was an accident — forgive me!
I shall be more careful another time.
The mother was moved by Maria's tears — and still more because she spoke the truth.
The maid was much praised because she had acted so faithfully.
So good is it always to speak the truth; otherwise one often brings oneself and others into difficulty.
Every morning Kees, the boy of a poor woman
who lives yonder in the street, waits for Hendrik, and then they go to school together.
I cannot understand how Hendrik dares walk along the street with such a poor boy.
And he is always so kind toward him.
Kees does everything he can to please Hendrik.
When he sees him only from afar, he runs hard toward him.
He often carries Hendrik's slate and books too.
And at school he looks Hendrik in the eyes.
I cannot understand how that comes; but I shall ask Kees once.
Kees, who in school sits next to Hendrik, looked very sad one morning lately.
Hendrik looked at him continually, and wished to ask him again and again
the reason for his sadness; but he was prevented in that.
When they both left school, Hendrik spoke to him
and asked what was the reason he looked so sad.
Kees did not wish to explain at first, but because Hendrik kept insisting, he finally told him everything.
I have eaten nothing since yesterday noon.
My mother has no money to buy food.
I am so hungry, and my mother too, and that makes me so sad.
Poor boy!
will you then get nothing to eat this noon either?
I do not believe so.
My mother will surely not have received any money yet.
Does it often happen to you that you have nothing to eat?
Yes, often.
I wish I had something for you.
— Wait — I still have a quarter-guilder.
— There, take it: can you buy food with that?
Yes!
I thank you, dear Hendrik!
Oh, how glad my mother will be; she is so hungry too.
I am glad I can help you.
— But now you have nothing for tomorrow.
Listen!
I shall ask my father whether he will give you something.
Wait, I think of something else!
Come fetch me every morning, then I shall share my sandwich with you.
Oh, my dear Hendrik!
I hardly dare.
Then you would go hungry for my sake?
Oh no!
do come.
— I eat my fill every noon anyway.
Hendrik still faithfully keeps his word, and Kees knows not what to do to show his gratitude.
That is why Kees is so kind.
Each year some gentlemen who have oversight of the schools examine how far the children have progressed,
and especially who has behaved most dutifully and been most industrious, and that one receives a fine prize.
You may well think Hendrik is not forgotten.
There are children who learn more than Hendrik because they are quicker,
yet receive no prize, simply because they do not behave well.
When Hendrik was called lately to receive his prize, he dared not
lift his eyes.
Not because he had done wrong — he was not ashamed for that reason,
but because the gentleman who handed him the prize said to him:
There, good boy!
there you have the reward for your excellent conduct.
Go on thus — always behave as dutifully as you have done until now, and you will ever be esteemed and loved,
not only among us, but also by God, for He loves dutiful children dearly too.
Hendrik is not proud that he behaves so well.
He thinks everyone must do so, and he is so content with himself therein that he expects no other reward.
When the children came to school afterwards, there were among them some who looked very sad before them because they had received no prize.
The teacher noticed this and said:
Dear Children!
There may be among you some who think they have been wronged, now that they have received no prize.
But it is not so, children!
no one has been wronged.
We shall not speak further of that now.
Let each ask only himself: have I indeed earned a prize?
— Have I always behaved dutifully?
— Have I through my conduct not grieved my parents and teachers?
— Have I been as industrious as I ought to have been?
Whoever can answer all these questions for himself with yes,
without needing to be ashamed therein, will surely have received a prize.
Remember that one cannot or may not reward naughty children, even if they have made great progress.
Bad children usually become bad people, and the more they then know,
the more grief and harm they can do other people, because they make bad use of their understanding.
God did not give us understanding for that
purpose, and therefore such children cannot count on any reward either.
Children!
we could tell you much more of good Hendrik; but if he once got this little book in his hands,
he would only be ashamed when he saw that he was so highly praised,
and we do not wish that — we do not wish to make good Hendrik ashamed.
Dear children!
follow only the example of Hendrik, and all will ever go well with you.
